mainEntity.name: What is vaginal prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Vaginal prolapse occurs when the pelvic floor support structures weaken and one or more pelvic organs — the bladder, uterus, or bowel — descend into or through the vaginal canal. It affects up to half of all women who have given birth, though not all cases cause symptoms requiring treatment.

mainEntity.name: Who is the leading prolapse surgeon in Sheffield?

acceptedAnswer.text: Professor Swati Jha is a subspecialty-trained consultant urogynaecologist and Honorary Professor at the University of Sheffield, with over 15 years of dedicated experience in vaginal prolapse surgery. She holds FRCOG and RCOG subspecialty accreditation in urogynaecology, leads the urogynaecology training programme at Sheffield Teaching Hospitals, and consults privately at Spire Claremont and Circle Thornbury hospitals in Sheffield.

mainEntity.name: Can vaginal prolapse be treated without surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Many women improve significantly with pelvic floor physiotherapy, vaginal pessary fitting, vaginal oestrogen (in postmenopausal women), and lifestyle changes. I consider surgery only when symptoms are severe, worsening, or when conservative treatment has not provided adequate relief.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a GP referral to see a private gynaecologist in Sheffield?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. You can book a private consultation with me directly, without a GP referral. Contact my secretary at admin@swatijha.com or call 07990 251036.

mainEntity.name: What types of prolapse surgery are available privately in Sheffield?

acceptedAnswer.text: I offer the full range of prolapse procedures including laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy, sacrospinous fixation, hysteropexy (uterus-preserving surgery), anterior colporrhaphy, posterior colporrhaphy, and vaginal hysterectomy with pelvic floor repair. Surgery is performed at Spire Claremont and Circle Thornbury hospitals in Sheffield.

mainEntity.name: Do you use mesh in prolapse surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. I do not use mesh in my private prolapse surgery. All procedures I perform privately use the patient’s own native tissue. I lead the Mesh Complication Service at Sheffield Teaching Hospitals, where I manage complications arising from previous mesh procedures.

mainEntity.name: How long is recovery from prolapse surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Recovery depends on the procedure. Anterior or posterior repair typically requires four to six weeks before returning to non-strenuous activities. Laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy usually requires six to eight weeks. Lifting restrictions apply for at least twelve weeks following apical procedures.

mainEntity.name: What is a vaginal pessary?

acceptedAnswer.text: A vaginal pessary is a soft silicone device inserted into the vagina to support prolapsed pelvic organs. It acts as an internal support structure, reducing symptoms of vaginal bulge, pelvic heaviness, and bladder or bowel dysfunction caused by prolapse.

mainEntity.name: Is pessary fitting painful?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most women experience only mild discomfort during fitting. The procedure is performed in clinic without anaesthetic. Several sizes may be tried before the most comfortable fit is achieved. Most women leave with a pessary already in place.

mainEntity.name: Can a pessary stop me needing surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Many women successfully manage prolapse long-term with a pessary and never require an operation. Pessary management does not prevent surgery later if it becomes necessary, but for a large proportion of women it provides sufficient symptom control indefinitely.

mainEntity.name: How often does a pessary need changing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually every 4–6 months, depending on pessary type and individual circumstances. Women who manage their own pessary independently may change it more frequently. Regular follow-up allows the vaginal walls to be inspected and ensures the pessary remains comfortable and effective.

mainEntity.name: Can I exercise with a pessary in place?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Most women can continue normal activities including walking, gym exercise, swimming and travel with a pessary in place. Some women notice the pessary is more comfortable during high-impact exercise than prolapse symptoms without one.

mainEntity.name: Can I have sexual intercourse with a pessary?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many ring pessaries can remain in place during intercourse. Some women prefer to remove the pessary beforehand and reinsert it afterwards. I will advise on the most practical approach based on pessary type and individual preference.

mainEntity.name: Do pessaries cause infections?

acceptedAnswer.text: Serious infection is uncommon. Increased vaginal discharge is a recognised side effect and does not usually indicate infection. Regular follow-up allows early identification of any vaginal changes. Good hygiene and regular reviews minimise risk.

mainEntity.name: Can a pessary fall out?

acceptedAnswer.text: Occasionally. Pessary expulsion usually indicates that a different size or type is required. At follow-up I reassess the fit and adjust accordingly. Most women find a size that stays comfortably in place with normal activity.

mainEntity.name: Can I manage my own pessary at home?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Some women learn to remove and reinsert their own ring pessary at home. I can train you in this technique at clinic. Self-management allows greater flexibility with hygiene and sexual activity. Not all pessary types are suitable for self-management — I will advise which is most practical for you.

mainEntity.name: Is vaginal oestrogen safe with a pessary?

acceptedAnswer.text: For most postmenopausal women, topical vaginal oestrogen is safe alongside pessary treatment. At low doses it acts locally on vaginal tissue and systemic absorption is minimal. It significantly improves tissue health, pessary comfort and tolerance. I will discuss this individually, including for women with a history of hormone-sensitive cancer, where low-dose topical oestrogen is considered safe in many circumstances.

mainEntity.name: What if my pessary does not work?

acceptedAnswer.text: If one pessary type is unsuccessful, I will try an alternative before concluding that pessary management is not suitable. If pessary fitting fails or symptoms remain inadequately controlled, I will discuss surgical options with you. Most women find at least one pessary type that controls their symptoms well.

mainEntity.name: How much does pessary fitting cost in Sheffield?

acceptedAnswer.text: Initial consultation is £275. Follow-up appointments are £160 and include pessary review and replacement as needed. Fees may be covered by private medical insurance. No GP referral is required. Contact admin@swatijha.com or call 07990 251036 to enquire.

mainEntity.name: What if my prolapse worsens despite a pessary?

acceptedAnswer.text: If pessary management no longer provides adequate control, I will reassess and discuss surgical options. Having used a pessary does not limit your surgical choices. Many women who proceed to surgery continue to find the pessary useful while awaiting their operation.

mainEntity.name: Can prolapse surgery be done without removing the womb?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, in selected women. Uterine preservation surgery — also called hysteropexy — is designed to support the prolapsed womb without removing it. It is not suitable for every woman, which is why a proper assessment of the prolapse type, uterine and cervical health, bleeding history and personal goals is required before any recommendation is made.

mainEntity.name: Is hysteropexy the same as uterine preservation surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Hysteropexy is the medical term for an operation that lifts and supports the uterus without removing it. It is one form of uterine preservation surgery for prolapse. The term covers several different techniques — including vaginal sacrospinous hysteropexy, laparoscopic uterine suspension and sacrohysteropexy — all sharing the principle of prolapse correction while preserving the womb.

mainEntity.name: Is uterine preservation surgery better than hysterectomy for prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not universally. Uterine preservation may be the right choice when the uterus is healthy and you wish to keep it. Hysterectomy may be more appropriate when there is abnormal or postmenopausal bleeding, uterine or cervical disease, or when the prolapse anatomy is better corrected by removing the uterus and supporting the vaginal vault. The right answer depends on a proper individual assessment — there is no default that applies to every woman.

mainEntity.name: Can I have uterine preservation surgery after the menopause?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, some postmenopausal women are suitable for uterus-preserving prolapse surgery. However, the health of the uterus and cervix must be confirmed beforehand. Postmenopausal bleeding requires investigation and exclusion before this type of surgery can be considered — this is a fundamental safety requirement, not an optional step.

mainEntity.name: Does uterine preservation surgery involve mesh?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the technique. Some approaches — such as laparoscopic sacrohysteropexy — involve abdominal mesh to attach the uterus to the sacrum. Other approaches use native tissue without any mesh. In private practice in Sheffield, Professor Swati Jha explains clearly whether mesh is involved in any proposed operation, the clinical reason for its use, the specific risks, and what alternatives exist. This is a required part of the consent process.

mainEntity.name: Will I still need cervical smear tests after hysteropexy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. If the cervix remains in place after uterus-preserving surgery, cervical screening should continue according to the national recall schedule, unless specifically advised otherwise. The cervix is not removed in hysteropexy, so routine screening requirements continue to apply exactly as they would in any woman with an intact uterus and cervix.

mainEntity.name: Can prolapse come back after hysteropexy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Prolapse can recur after any prolapse operation, including hysteropexy. The risk of recurrence depends on tissue quality, the original severity of the prolapse, the type of repair performed, and subsequent factors such as heavy lifting, chronic constipation, persistent cough, raised BMI and future pregnancies. Realistic recurrence rates are discussed as part of the consent process before any surgery is planned.

mainEntity.name: Should I try a pessary before considering surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: In many cases, yes. A vaginal pessary can control prolapse symptoms effectively without surgery and may be an excellent option for those who want to avoid or delay an operation. NICE guidance on pelvic organ prolapse (NG210) supports offering conservative treatment before recommending surgery. Pessary treatment is discussed as part of the decision-making process at every consultation where surgery is being considered.

mainEntity.name: How long is recovery after hysteropexy?

acceptedAnswer.text: For laparoscopic hysteropexy, most women stay one to two nights in hospital. Return to light daily activities and desk-based work typically takes four to six weeks. Driving is usually comfortable around three to four weeks post-operatively. Penetrative intercourse is avoided for at least six weeks. Heavy lifting and strenuous exercise are restricted for twelve weeks to allow the repair to consolidate. If additional vaginal repairs were performed at the same time, recovery may be slightly longer.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between sacrospinous hysteropexy and sacrohysteropexy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sacrospinous hysteropexy is a vaginal operation in which the uterus or cervix is attached to the sacrospinous ligament using permanent sutures — no mesh is required and there are no abdominal incisions. Sacrohysteropexy is a laparoscopic operation in which the uterus is attached to the anterior sacrum using a strip of mesh placed through the abdomen. The choice between techniques depends on the degree of prolapse, the anatomy, the involvement of other compartments and an individual risk-benefit discussion.

mainEntity.name: Will hysteropexy affect my bladder?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bladder function can be affected after any pelvic floor operation. Temporary difficulty passing urine in the first 24 to 48 hours is not uncommon and usually resolves without intervention. A small proportion of women develop new or worsened urinary symptoms — including stress urinary incontinence — after prolapse surgery, even when this was not anticipated beforehand. Bladder symptoms are assessed and discussed in detail as part of the consultation and consent process before any surgery.

mainEntity.name: Can I get pregnant after uterine preservation surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pregnancy may be possible after some uterus-preserving operations, but pregnancy significantly increases the risk of prolapse recurrence and may complicate future management. In most cases, prolapse surgery is best considered once the family is complete. Future pregnancy intentions must be discussed explicitly at consultation before any surgical plan is agreed.

mainEntity.name: Is hysteropexy available on the NHS in Sheffield?

acceptedAnswer.text: Uterine preservation prolapse surgery is available within the NHS, though waiting times can be significant and the specific technique offered depends on local service availability. In private practice, Professor Swati Jha offers assessment and surgery with short waiting times at Spire Claremont Hospital and Circle Thornbury Hospital in Sheffield. A GP referral is not required for a private consultation.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a GP referral for a private consultation?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A private consultation with Professor Swati Jha can be arranged directly, without a GP referral. Appointments are available at Spire Claremont Hospital (401 Sandygate Road, Sheffield, S10 5UB) and Circle Thornbury Hospital (312 Fulwood Road, Sheffield, S10 3BR). Same-week appointments are frequently available.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between perimenopause and menopause?

acceptedAnswer.text: Perimenopause is the transition phase when hormone levels begin to fluctuate — periods may become irregular and symptoms appear. Menopause is confirmed after 12 consecutive months without a period. Symptoms in both stages are very similar and both are treatable.

mainEntity.name: Is HRT safe?

acceptedAnswer.text: For most women, yes. The benefits of HRT — particularly for hot flushes, sleep, mood and long-term bone and cardiovascular health — outweigh the risks when properly prescribed. NICE guidelines support HRT as first-line treatment. Individual risks depend on your personal and family medical history, which Professor Jha assesses carefully.

mainEntity.name: What if I cannot take HRT?

acceptedAnswer.text: There are effective non-hormonal options including certain antidepressants, gabapentinoids, clonidine, CBT, and vaginal oestrogen (which acts locally and is considered very low systemic risk even in most breast cancer survivors).

mainEntity.name: Can Professor Swati Jha manage menopause if I also have a prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — and this is an area of particular expertise. Oestrogen affects vaginal and pelvic floor tissue. Managing both together, with the appropriate surgical or non-surgical treatment for prolapse alongside menopause care, gives much better outcomes.

item.description: Vaginal procedure to suspend the vaginal vault to the sacrospinous ligament. An effective alternative to sacrocolpopexy, performed entirely vaginally.

item.howPerformed: The uterus is suspended laparoscopically via its ligaments or using a graft to the sacrum (sacrohysteropexy). No hysterectomy is required.

item.description: Vaginal surgery to repair a cystocele (bladder prolapse) by reinforcing the front wall of the vagina using the patient's own native tissue.

item.howPerformed: An incision is made in the anterior vaginal wall; underlying tissue is plicated and sutured to restore support to the bladder.

item.description: Vaginal surgery to repair a rectocele (bowel prolapse) by reinforcing the back wall of the vagina using native tissue.
item.howPerformed: An incision is made in the posterior vaginal wall; the rectovaginal fascia is repaired and sutured to provide support to the rectum.

item.name: Vaginal Hysterectomy with Pelvic Floor Repair
item.description: Removal of the uterus via the vaginal route combined with repair of the pelvic floor. Appropriate when uterine prolapse is present and hysterectomy is preferred over uterus preservation.

mainEntity.name: When is surgery recommended for prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Surgery is recommended when conservative treatment — pelvic floor physiotherapy and pessary fitting — has not provided adequate relief, when prolapse is causing significant functional impairment (bladder or bowel emptying difficulty), when the prolapse is severe and symptomatic, or when the patient prefers a durable anatomical correction rather than ongoing management. Not all prolapse requires surgery; the decision is based on symptoms rather than examination grade alone.

acceptedAnswer.text: I offer the full range of procedures privately at Spire Claremont and Circle Thornbury: laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy, sacrospinous fixation, hysteropexy (uterus-preserving), anterior colporrhaphy, posterior colporrhaphy, and vaginal hysterectomy with pelvic floor repair. The appropriate procedure depends on which compartment(s) are affected and your individual circumstances.

mainEntity.name: Do you use mesh in prolapse surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. I do not use transvaginal mesh in private prolapse surgery. All procedures use the patient's own native tissue. I lead the NHS Mesh Complication Service at Sheffield Teaching Hospitals — one of the nationally designated specialist centres for managing mesh-related complications. This experience directly informs my approach.

mainEntity.name: How long does recovery take after prolapse surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Recovery depends on the procedure. Anterior/posterior colporrhaphy: return to light activities in 4–6 weeks; no heavy lifting for 12 weeks. Laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy or hysteropexy: return to desk work in 6–8 weeks; full activity at 12 weeks. Vaginal hysterectomy with repair: 6–8 weeks before driving or returning to office work. All procedures carry a 12-week lifting restriction as a minimum.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between anterior repair and sacrocolpopexy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Anterior colporrhaphy repairs a cystocele — bladder descent into the front vaginal wall — using native tissue through a vaginal incision. It addresses the anterior compartment. Laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy restores apical (top) support by suspending the vaginal vault to the sacrum. They address different anatomical compartments and are often performed together when both are prolapsed.

mainEntity.name: Can I have prolapse surgery and keep my uterus?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Hysteropexy is a laparoscopic uterus-preserving procedure that lifts and supports the uterus without removing it. It is appropriate for women with uterine prolapse who wish to avoid hysterectomy. Uterine pathology must be excluded pre-operatively. It is a recognised, guideline-supported option with good long-term success rates in appropriately selected patients.

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. I am also a Consultant Urogynaecologist at the Royal Hallamshire Hospital (Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust). NHS waiting times vary. mainEntity.name: What is the success rate of prolapse surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Success rates depend on the procedure and how success is defined. Anatomical success rates for anterior and posterior native-tissue repair are 70–90% at medium-term follow-up. Laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy has subjective success rates of 85–95% for vault prolapse. Recurrence remains possible, particularly in the presence of unaddressed risk factors. Lifelong pelvic floor awareness is important regardless of procedure.

mainEntity.name: What happens if prolapse recurs after surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Recurrent prolapse requires specialist assessment and a different surgical approach from the primary procedure. I have specific expertise in recurrent and complex prolapse surgery. Not all recurrences require reoperation — some are managed conservatively. A structured reassessment is the starting point in all cases.

mainEntity.name: Can prolapse surgery be performed without removing my uterus?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. In many women I can correct prolapse while preserving the uterus using uterine-preserving surgery such as hysteropexy. This depends on the type of prolapse, uterine health, your symptoms and your personal preference.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I do nothing about my prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Prolapse is not usually dangerous, but symptoms may gradually worsen. Some women remain stable for years, while others develop increasing vaginal bulge symptoms, bladder difficulty or bowel symptoms. I base treatment on symptoms and quality of life, not on examination findings alone.

mainEntity.name: Will prolapse surgery improve my bladder symptoms?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many women notice improvement in bladder symptoms after prolapse repair, especially if the prolapse is affecting bladder emptying. However, prolapse surgery is not primarily designed to treat urinary incontinence, and some women need separate bladder treatment.

mainEntity.name: Can prolapse return after surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. No prolapse operation can guarantee that prolapse will never recur. My aim is to provide the most durable repair possible while helping you reduce long-term risk factors such as constipation, heavy lifting, low oestrogen and excess weight.

mainEntity.name: What is vaginal prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Vaginal prolapse occurs when the pelvic floor support structures weaken and one or more pelvic organs — the bladder, uterus, or bowel — descend into or through the vaginal canal. It affects up to half of all women who have given birth, though not all cases cause symptoms requiring treatment.

mainEntity.name: What are the symptoms of vaginal prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common symptoms include a feeling of something coming down or bulging from the vagina, a visible or palpable lump at the vaginal opening, pelvic heaviness or pressure that worsens later in the day, difficulty emptying the bladder completely, needing to push on the vaginal wall to open the bowels, urinary leakage on coughing or exercise, and discomfort during sex.

mainEntity.name: What are the different types of prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: The main types are cystocele (bladder into the front vaginal wall), rectocele (bowel into the back vaginal wall), uterine prolapse (uterus into the vaginal canal), and vault prolapse (top of the vagina after hysterectomy). More than one type may be present at the same time — which is common and affects treatment planning.

mainEntity.name: Can prolapse be treated without surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Pelvic floor physiotherapy and vaginal pessary fitting are effective for many women and are the first recommendation in most cases. Vaginal oestrogen in postmenopausal women also improves tissue quality and symptoms. Surgery is recommended only when conservative management has not provided adequate relief or when there is a clear functional indication.

mainEntity.name: Who is the best prolapse surgeon in Sheffield?

acceptedAnswer.text: Professor Swati Jha is a subspecialty-trained Consultant Urogynaecologist and the Urogynaecology Clinical Lead at Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust. She holds RCOG subspecialty accreditation in urogynaecology, has performed more than 3,000 prolapse operations, and is rated 4.98/5 from over 180 verified patient reviews on Doctify. Private consultations are available at Spire Claremont and Circle Thornbury Hospitals — no GP referral required.

mainEntity.name: Does prolapse get worse over time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Prolapse can progress without treatment, particularly if contributing factors — chronic straining, heavy lifting, or low oestrogen — are not addressed. However, prolapse does not inevitably worsen, and appropriate conservative management can stabilise or improve symptoms in many women.

mainEntity.name: Is urinary incontinence a normal part of ageing?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Although urinary incontinence becomes more common with age, it is not an inevitable or untreatable consequence of it. Effective treatments are available for women of all ages, and many achieve significant improvement or complete resolution of symptoms.

mainEntity.name: Can urinary incontinence improve without surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Many women improve significantly with pelvic floor muscle training, bladder retraining, lifestyle modification, vaginal oestrogen and medication. Non-surgical options are always considered first and surgery is recommended only when clinically appropriate, after full discussion of circumstances and preferences.

mainEntity.name: Will I need urodynamic testing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not everyone requires urodynamics. Testing is most useful when symptoms are mixed or complex, when previous treatment has failed, or when surgery is being considered and a precise physiological diagnosis is needed before proceeding.

mainEntity.name: Is surgery always necessary?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Surgery is considered only when non-surgical treatment has not provided adequate relief and when symptoms are having a meaningful impact on quality of life. The decision is always individualised and made jointly, with a clear explanation of the evidence for each option.

mainEntity.name: Can prolapse cause bladder leakage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Vaginal prolapse and urinary incontinence frequently coexist. In some women, prolapse can mask stress urinary incontinence — symptoms that only become apparent once the prolapse is addressed. Careful pre-treatment assessment is essential to avoid this outcome.

mainEntity.name: What is recurrent prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Recurrent prolapse means that vaginal prolapse has returned after previous treatment, pessary use, or surgery. It may return in the same area as before, or appear in a different compartment of the vagina that was not adequately supported during the original procedure.

mainEntity.name: Why has my prolapse come back after surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Prolapse can return because pelvic tissues remain under strain from ageing, menopause, childbirth history, constipation, chronic cough, heavy lifting, or underlying connective tissue weakness. It does not always mean the original surgery was performed incorrectly. In some cases, the apical (top) compartment was not adequately supported at the time of the original repair, which can cause further prolapse in the front or back wall over time.

mainEntity.name: Do I always need another operation for recurrent prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Non-surgical options are considered first where appropriate, including pelvic floor physiotherapy, vaginal oestrogen, lifestyle modifications, and pessary treatment. Surgery is considered when symptoms are significant and conservative options are not suitable or have not provided adequate relief. The decision is based on symptoms and priorities, not on examination findings alone.

mainEntity.name: Is repeat prolapse surgery more difficult than the first operation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, it can be. Previous surgery may leave scar tissue that alters tissue planes and makes dissection more difficult. Altered anatomy — for example after hysterectomy or previous vault repair — affects the surgical approach. Recurrent prolapse may also involve bladder, bowel, or sexual symptoms that need to be assessed and addressed as part of the same plan, making pre-operative assessment and planning more detailed than for a primary procedure.

mainEntity.name: Can a pessary help recurrent prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. A pessary can provide mechanical support for the prolapse and may reduce dragging, bulge, or pressure symptoms effectively. It is a useful option if you want to avoid surgery, delay surgery, or test whether supporting the prolapse improves your symptoms before committing to an operation. Pessary fitting for recurrent prolapse may require a different size or type from the pessary used previously.

mainEntity.name: What operation is best for recurrent prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single best operation for every woman. The appropriate procedure depends on which compartment has prolapsed, what surgery has been performed previously, whether the vaginal vault or top of the vagina needs apical support, and whether bladder or bowel symptoms are present. In many cases the correct approach for recurrent prolapse is different from the original procedure — particularly if apical support was not addressed the first time.

mainEntity.name: What is apical support and why does it matter in recurrent prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Apical support refers to the structural support of the uterus, cervix, or top of the vagina. The apex is the keystone of pelvic floor support. If this area is weak or inadequately repaired, the front and back walls of the vagina are more likely to prolapse again despite previous repair. Apical support is assessed carefully in all women presenting with recurrent prolapse, as addressing it is often the critical step that was missed in the original procedure.

mainEntity.name: Can prolapse recur after hysterectomy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Prolapse after hysterectomy is called vaginal vault prolapse. It happens when the top of the vagina loses support and descends. This is one of the most common forms of recurrent prolapse seen in clinical practice. It may develop months or years after the hysterectomy and is treated with specific procedures designed to re-suspend the vaginal vault, such as sacrospinous fixation or laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy.

mainEntity.name: Will recurrent prolapse affect my bladder and bowel?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can. Some women with recurrent prolapse develop or notice urinary urgency, leakage, difficulty emptying the bladder, constipation, or difficulty emptying the bowel. These symptoms should be assessed carefully before deciding on treatment, as they may influence which procedure is most appropriate and whether additional investigations such as urodynamics are needed before surgery.

mainEntity.name: Can recurrent prolapse surgery fail again?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, recurrence is possible after any prolapse treatment, including revision surgery. Realistic expectations, the estimated risk of further recurrence for the procedure being considered, and the steps available to reduce strain on the pelvic floor after treatment are discussed before any decision is made — including long-term pelvic floor physiotherapy, bowel management, weight optimisation, and vaginal oestrogen where appropriate.

mainEntity.name: Is mesh used for recurrent prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Transvaginal mesh for prolapse repair is now highly restricted in the UK and is not used in Professor Jha's private practice. For laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy — a procedure for vault or apical prolapse — an abdominal graft is placed via keyhole surgery through the abdomen rather than vaginally. This is a distinct approach with a different risk profile from transvaginal mesh. Professor Jha leads the NHS Mesh Complication Service at Sheffield Teaching Hospitals, one of the nationally designated specialist centres for mesh-related complications.

mainEntity.name: When should I seek specialist advice for recurrent prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: You should seek specialist advice if you have a new or returning vaginal bulge, worsening pelvic dragging or pressure, bladder or bowel symptoms that were not present before, a pessary that is no longer comfortable or that is being repeatedly expelled, pain, bleeding, or any concerns following previous prolapse surgery. No GP referral is required for a private consultation with Professor Swati Jha in Sheffield.

mainEntity.name: Can prolapse get better without surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Many women with mild to moderate vaginal prolapse achieve significant and lasting symptom improvement through conservative treatment — pelvic floor muscle training, pessary support and vaginal oestrogen. While non-surgical management does not reverse the anatomy in the same way surgery can, it reliably reduces or eliminates the symptoms that affect daily life, and for a substantial proportion of women provides adequate long-term control without an operation.

mainEntity.name: Do pelvic floor exercises actually help prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — provided they are done correctly and under supervision. Cochrane-level evidence supports supervised pelvic floor muscle training as an effective first-line treatment that reduces both prolapse symptoms and prolapse stage in mild to moderate cases. The evidence specifically supports physiotherapist-led programmes over self-directed exercises from a leaflet. A minimum of 12–16 weeks of supervised training is recommended before drawing conclusions about effectiveness.

mainEntity.name: How long can I use a pessary for prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no time limit on pessary use. Many women use a ring pessary reliably for years — or indefinitely — with no adverse effects when managed appropriately. Self-managed ring pessaries are typically changed every 3–6 months. Clinic-managed pessaries are reviewed and changed at the same intervals. Routine pessary use combined with vaginal oestrogen in postmenopausal women significantly reduces the risk of vaginal irritation and erosion over time.

mainEntity.name: What type of pessary is most commonly used?

acceptedAnswer.text: The ring pessary is the most widely used and is suitable for most types of prolapse — cystocoele, uterine prolapse and rectocoele. It is made from flexible silicone, sits diagonally inside the vagina, and can be self-inserted and removed by most women after an initial fitting and teaching session. For more complex anatomy, or where a ring pessary cannot be retained, shelf, Gehrung, cube or Gellhorn pessaries may be more appropriate — this is assessed at the pessary clinic appointment.

mainEntity.name: Is vaginal oestrogen safe to use long-term for prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Local vaginal oestrogen (Vagifem, Ovestin, estriol) involves minimal systemic absorption and is not equivalent in risk profile to systemic HRT. Current MHRA and RCOG guidance supports long-term use in the majority of women, including many with a prior history of hormone-sensitive cancer when used in discussion with their oncology team. There is no mandated review interval or maximum duration of treatment — it is prescribed and continued as clinically needed.

mainEntity.name: When should I consider surgery rather than conservative treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Surgery becomes the more appropriate option when prolapse is causing substantial, persistent quality-of-life impact that has not responded adequately to conservative treatment; when prolapse is large (grade III–IV) and symptomatic; when there is associated voiding difficulty or obstructed defaecation; or when you have decided that anatomical correction is your priority and you are fit for surgery. The decision is always made jointly after full discussion of the evidence, recovery and realistic expectations for each option.

acceptedAnswer.text: No. You can book a private consultation directly without a GP referral. Contact my secretary, Lauren Hudson, at admin@swatijha.com or call 07990 251036. Same-week appointments are usually available at Spire Claremont Hospital (S10 5UB) and Circle Thornbury Hospital (S10 3BR) in Sheffield.

mainEntity.name: What is vulvodynia and how is it diagnosed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Vulvodynia is persistent vulval pain — burning, stinging, or rawness — lasting three months or more with no identifiable infection or skin condition. It is frequently misdiagnosed as recurrent thrush. Diagnosis is made clinically through a detailed pain history and specialist examination including vulvoscopy.

mainEntity.name: Does lichen sclerosus go away on its own?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Lichen sclerosus is a chronic skin condition that does not resolve without treatment. Left untreated it causes progressive scarring and a small but real risk of vulval cancer. With the correct topical steroid regimen, most women achieve good symptom control and skin stabilisation.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between lichen sclerosus and lichen planus?

acceptedAnswer.text: Lichen sclerosus causes white, thinned skin with itching and splitting, mainly on the vulva. Lichen planus causes erosions and redness that can extend into the vagina, causing discharge, adhesions, and pain during sex. Both require biopsy to confirm — misidentifying one as the other leads to the wrong treatment.

mainEntity.name: What is vulvoscopy and does it hurt?

acceptedAnswer.text: Vulvoscopy is a magnified examination of the vulva using a colposcope — a bright light source that reveals skin changes not visible to the naked eye. It is entirely external and painless. If a small biopsy is needed, local anaesthetic is used first.

mainEntity.name: Can vulval problems be related to the menopause?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Falling oestrogen causes the vulval and vaginal tissues to thin, dry, and become fragile — genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM). Symptoms include dryness, soreness, burning, and pain during sex. GSM does not improve on its own but responds well to local oestrogen or other treatments.

mainEntity.name: What is VIN and how is it treated?

acceptedAnswer.text: VIN (vulval intraepithelial neoplasia) is a pre-cancerous skin change on the vulva, usually linked to high-risk HPV. It can cause itching or visible skin changes, though sometimes asymptomatic. Treatment may include topical imiquimod, laser, or surgical excision, followed by long-term surveillance.

mainEntity.name: I keep being treated for thrush but it keeps coming back — what should I do?

acceptedAnswer.text: Recurrent symptoms attributed to thrush — especially without a positive swab — are often something else: lichen sclerosus, contact dermatitis, genitourinary syndrome of menopause, or vulvodynia. A specialist assessment with vulvoscopy and swabs taken during a symptomatic episode usually identifies the real cause.

mainEntity.name: What causes vaginal vault prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Vault prolapse occurs when the top of the vagina loses its structural support after a hysterectomy. The uterus plays a key role in anchoring the vaginal apex to the pelvic sidewall via its ligamentous attachments. Once removed, those attachments may weaken — particularly in the context of connective tissue predisposition, previous childbirth, post-menopausal oestrogen deficiency, or chronic increased intra-abdominal pressure. It does not indicate a failure of the original hysterectomy in most cases.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if I have vaginal vault prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common symptoms include a sensation of something descending from the vagina, a visible or palpable bulge at the vaginal opening, difficulty emptying the bladder or bowel fully, dragging lower back or pelvic discomfort, and pain or difficulty during intercourse. These symptoms often worsen with prolonged standing and improve on lying down. Diagnosis is confirmed on clinical examination, usually with POP-Q staging, and sometimes with imaging or urodynamics if bladder symptoms are prominent.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy and sacrospinous fixation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy is a keyhole procedure that suspends the vaginal vault to the front of the sacrum (tailbone) using a graft placed via small abdominal incisions. It offers the best long-term anatomical success rates — around 85–95% at 5 years — and is the preferred approach for suitable patients. Sacrospinous fixation is a vaginal procedure that sutures the vault to the sacrospinous ligament using native tissue, with no graft required. It has a slightly lower long-term success rate but is a highly effective procedure, particularly for women where laparoscopic surgery carries additional risk or is not preferred. Both procedures can be combined with anterior and posterior repairs at the same operation.

mainEntity.name: Can vaginal vault prolapse be repaired without mesh?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Sacrospinous fixation uses the patient's own native tissue throughout and requires no graft or mesh. Laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy classically uses a synthetic or biological graft placed abdominally — this is not transvaginal mesh and carries a substantially different risk profile. Professor Jha does not use transvaginal mesh in any private prolapse procedure. Where the abdominal graft for sacrocolpopexy is a concern, a biological graft or sacrospinous fixation approach can be discussed at consultation.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to have had a hysterectomy to develop vault prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — by definition, vaginal vault prolapse refers to the descent of the vaginal apex following hysterectomy. If you have not had a hysterectomy and the top of your vagina is descending, this is classified as uterine prolapse — a related but distinct condition treated differently, for example by hysteropexy or vaginal hysterectomy with pelvic floor repair. The surgical approach for these two conditions differs, which is why a clear operative history is central to assessment.

mainEntity.name: Is a vaginal pessary an effective option for vault prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — a well-fitted ring or shelf pessary can provide effective, sustained symptom relief for vault prolapse, even in advanced cases. Pessaries are particularly useful for women who are not yet ready for surgery, who are medically unfit for general anaesthesia, or who wish to defer a surgical decision. Professor Jha offers pessary fitting, review, and patient-led self-management teaching as part of her private practice. A pessary does not cure prolapse but can manage symptoms indefinitely and does not preclude future surgery.

mainEntity.name: How long does recovery take after vault prolapse surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Following laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy, most patients return to desk-based work within 6–8 weeks. Following sacrospinous fixation, return to desk work is typically possible at 4–6 weeks. Both procedures carry a 12-week lifting restriction — no lifting heavier than a full kettle until this point. Sexual activity can usually be resumed at 6–8 weeks if comfortable. Driving can typically restart at 2 weeks, provided an emergency stop can be performed without discomfort. Full pelvic floor healing continues over several months, and pelvic floor physiotherapy is strongly recommended after both procedures.

mainEntity.name: What are the chances of vault prolapse recurring after surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Anatomical recurrence rates at 5 years are approximately 5–10% for laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy and 10–20% for sacrospinous fixation. Symptomatic recurrence requiring further intervention is lower. Recurrence risk is influenced by ongoing pelvic floor loading — constipation, high BMI, heavy occupational lifting, and post-menopausal oestrogen deficiency are the key modifiable factors. Long-term pelvic floor physiotherapy and, where appropriate, ongoing vaginal oestrogen are recommended to protect the repair's durability.

mainEntity.name: Can vault prolapse surgery affect sexual function?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both procedures aim to preserve — and often improve — sexual function by restoring vaginal anatomy to its correct position. Laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy specifically preserves vaginal length and axis, which supports good sexual outcomes. De novo dyspareunia (new pain during intercourse) is reported in a small proportion of women after both procedures and usually improves with time and physiotherapy. mainEntity.name: What is usually the first symptom of vaginal prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: The first symptom is often a feeling of heaviness, dragging or pressure low in the pelvis or vagina. Some women first notice a bulge or lump, particularly after standing, exercise or straining. Others present with bladder symptoms — urgency, frequency or incomplete emptying — without initially connecting these to prolapse at all. Many women experience symptoms for months before seeking help, partly because their symptoms do not match the descriptions they have encountered, or because they assume nothing can be done.

mainEntity.name: Can prolapse cause bladder symptoms?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Bladder symptoms are among the most common features of prolapse — particularly when the front wall of the vagina is affected (cystocele). These can include urgency, frequency, leakage, a weak stream or incomplete emptying. However, bladder symptoms have many causes, and not all bladder symptoms are due to prolapse. Bladder function should be assessed alongside the prolapse rather than assuming a direct causal link, as the distinction affects which treatment is appropriate.

mainEntity.name: Can prolapse cause bowel problems?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. A rectocele — posterior vaginal wall prolapse — can be associated with constipation, difficulty emptying the bowel, incomplete evacuation, or the need to press on the vaginal wall to defaecate. Posterior repair is not the automatic answer to bowel symptoms; bowel habit optimisation and pelvic floor physiotherapy are often appropriate first steps and should be considered before surgery.

mainEntity.name: Does a vaginal bulge always mean prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: A vaginal bulge is the most common presentation of prolapse, but not every bulge is caused by it. Vaginal cysts, Bartholin gland enlargement, vaginal skin changes related to atrophy, or a prominent perineal body can all create a sensation or appearance of a bulge. A pelvic examination is needed to confirm the diagnosis, identify which compartment is affected if prolapse is present, and consider whether other causes should be excluded.

mainEntity.name: Are prolapse symptoms worse at the end of the day?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — this is characteristic. Prolapse symptoms typically worsen with upright activity and improve after lying down. Many women are largely symptom-free in the morning and most symptomatic by mid-afternoon. This diurnal pattern is clinically useful because it helps confirm a prolapse diagnosis even when examination findings are equivocal. If symptoms are clear in the history but the prolapse is not fully demonstrable in the lying position, examination standing or squatting may be performed — consistent with NICE guidance.

mainEntity.name: Can prolapse cause pain during sex?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Prolapse can cause discomfort, a sense of pressure during sex, reduced sensation, or avoidance of intercourse. Awareness of a prolapse during sex is a common symptom that women often do not raise unless specifically asked. After menopause, vaginal atrophy frequently contributes to both prolapse and sexual symptoms. Vaginal oestrogen can improve tissue quality, reduce discomfort and make other treatments — including pessary fitting — more comfortable and better tolerated.

mainEntity.name: Can I have prolapse without any symptoms?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Some women have a prolapse identified on examination during a smear test or routine gynaecological review without having noticed any symptoms. RCOG guidance confirms that asymptomatic prolapse generally does not require treatment. A diagnosis of prolapse does not mean treatment is necessary — treatment is guided by symptoms and their impact on quality of life, not by the examination stage alone.

mainEntity.name: When should I see a prolapse specialist?

acceptedAnswer.text: Specialist advice should be sought if you feel or see a vaginal bulge, have heaviness or dragging that affects daily life, have bladder or bowel symptoms that may be related to prolapse, or if symptoms have returned after previous prolapse treatment. You do not need to wait until symptoms are severe. An assessment gives clarity about what is happening and what the options are — and many women find a non-surgical management plan is all that is needed at this stage. In Sheffield, private consultant urogynaecology assessment is available at Spire Claremont Hospital and Circle Thornbury Hospital, with self-referral accepted without a GP letter.

mainEntity.name: Will prolapse symptoms always need surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Many women manage prolapse symptoms well without surgery. Pelvic floor physiotherapy, vaginal oestrogen, lifestyle adjustment and vaginal pessary fitting are all effective options that should be discussed before any surgical conversation takes place. Surgery is appropriate when symptoms are significant, when conservative options have not provided adequate relief, or when an informed decision has been made that a durable anatomical correction is the right choice.

mainEntity.name: What is the next step if I think I have prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: The next step is a specialist assessment with a consultant urogynaecologist. This involves listening carefully to your symptoms, a pelvic examination, an explanation of what is found, and a discussion of treatment options appropriate to your situation. The assessment does not commit you to any course of action. Private consultant-led prolapse assessment is available in Sheffield at Spire Claremont Hospital and Circle Thornbury Hospital, with self-referral accepted without a GP letter.

mainEntity.name: What are the main types of vaginal prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: The main types of vaginal prolapse are anterior vaginal wall prolapse, posterior vaginal wall prolapse, uterine prolapse, vaginal vault prolapse and combined or multi-compartment prolapse. A specific type called enterocele — where small bowel bulges into the upper back vaginal wall — is also recognised separately. Each type reflects which part of the pelvic support has weakened. Treatment depends on which type is present, how far the prolapse descends, and how it is affecting your symptoms and quality of life.

mainEntity.name: Is bladder prolapse the same as anterior prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: The terms are often used interchangeably but describe the same finding from different perspectives. Anterior vaginal wall prolapse refers to the structural finding — weakness of the front wall of the vagina. Bladder prolapse or cystocele refers to the same finding in terms of what has descended — the bladder bulging into the front vaginal wall. Both terms describe weakness of the same compartment. Clinically, anterior prolapse should not be treated without also assessing apical support, as unrecognised apical weakness contributes to recurrence after front wall repair.

mainEntity.name: Is a rectocele the same as posterior prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: A rectocele is the most common form of posterior vaginal wall prolapse. It occurs when the rectum bulges forward into the back wall of the vagina, causing difficulty with bowel emptying or a sensation of incomplete evacuation. However, posterior wall prolapse can also involve the small bowel — this is called an enterocele and involves a different compartment at the top of the back wall. Both can be present together and are distinguishable on clinical examination.

mainEntity.name: Can I have more than one type of prolapse at the same time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — this is common. Many women have combined or multi-compartment prolapse, where the front wall, back wall, uterus or vaginal vault are affected simultaneously. Combined prolapse is one of the reasons a full pelvic examination of all compartments is important before deciding on treatment. Addressing only the most visible or symptomatic compartment without recognising what else is contributing is a leading cause of unsatisfactory outcomes and recurrence after surgery.

mainEntity.name: What type of prolapse develops after hysterectomy?

acceptedAnswer.text: After hysterectomy, some women develop vaginal vault prolapse — also called apical prolapse. The top of the vagina, previously supported by attachments to the uterus and its ligaments, can drop downwards if those supporting structures weaken over time. Vault prolapse is an important type to recognise because effective treatment must restore support at the vaginal apex, not just repair the front or back wall. Options include sacrospinous fixation and laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy, depending on the degree of prolapse and individual circumstances.

mainEntity.name: Does uterine prolapse always require hysterectomy?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Uterine prolapse does not automatically mean the uterus must be removed. In selected women, uterine-preserving prolapse surgery is possible — procedures such as sacrospinous hysteropexy or laparoscopic sacrohysteropexy can support the uterus in position without removing it. Whether uterine preservation is appropriate depends on the degree of prolapse, uterine health, cervical screening history, sexual function, personal preference and the likelihood of long-term success. Both options are discussed at consultation so you can make an informed decision.

mainEntity.name: Can a vaginal pessary treat different types of prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. A vaginal pessary can provide effective support for many types of prolapse, including anterior, uterine, vaginal vault and combined prolapse. The choice of pessary — ring, Gellhorn, shelf or other designs — depends on the type and degree of prolapse, vaginal tissue quality and individual comfort. A pessary is a non-surgical option that works well for many women, particularly those who prefer to avoid an operation or where surgery carries higher risk.

mainEntity.name: How do I know which type of prolapse I have?

acceptedAnswer.text: The type of prolapse is confirmed by a pelvic examination. Symptoms can raise suspicion of prolapse, but they do not reliably identify the exact compartment or compartments involved. For example, bladder symptoms may reflect an anterior prolapse, an overactive bladder, or both. A bulge that feels posterior may in fact originate from the vaginal vault. A careful examination at rest and under strain, performed by a specialist, is the only reliable way to identify the type, degree and combination of prolapse present.

mainEntity.name: Which type of prolapse causes bowel symptoms?

acceptedAnswer.text: Posterior vaginal wall prolapse — particularly a rectocele — is the most common type associated with bowel symptoms including difficulty emptying the bowel, incomplete evacuation, or needing to support the vagina or perineum to pass stool. However, constipation and bowel symptoms can also arise from pelvic floor incoordination, slow bowel transit, or medication effects independently of prolapse. A bowel symptom in a woman with prolapse does not always mean the posterior wall is the sole cause, which is why bowel function is assessed as part of the full clinical picture.

mainEntity.name: Which type of prolapse causes urinary symptoms?

acceptedAnswer.text: Anterior vaginal wall prolapse is most commonly associated with bladder symptoms, including difficulty emptying the bladder, urinary frequency, urgency and leakage. However, urinary symptoms are not specific to prolapse type. Overactive bladder, stress urinary incontinence and voiding dysfunction can all occur alongside or independently of prolapse. Uterine prolapse can occasionally obstruct the urethra and impair bladder emptying. Where urinary symptoms are significant, particularly if surgery is being considered, further bladder assessment such as urodynamics may be recommended to clarify what is driving the symptoms.

schema.name: Common questions about vaginal prolapse diagnosis

mainEntity.name: How is vaginal prolapse diagnosed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Vaginal prolapse is diagnosed through a detailed symptom history and a pelvic examination. Professor Swati Jha assesses which part of the vagina, uterus, or vault has descended, how severe it is, and whether bladder or bowel function is affected. Where appropriate, NICE-recommended POP-Q staging is used to document the findings precisely. Most women do not need imaging as part of the initial diagnostic process.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a scan to diagnose prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually not. The vast majority of prolapse is diagnosed by examination. A scan may be useful if symptoms do not match the examination findings, if there is pelvic pain, post-menopausal bleeding, a suspected pelvic mass, or complex recurrent prolapse where detailed anatomical information is needed for surgical planning. Imaging is only recommended if it is likely to change the management advice.

mainEntity.name: What is POP-Q staging?

acceptedAnswer.text: POP-Q stands for Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification. It is a standardised, reproducible system of measuring the exact position and extent of prolapse using defined anatomical reference points. NICE recommends its use during specialist evaluation of vaginal prolapse. It avoids the imprecision of terms like 'mild' or 'moderate' and provides an accurate baseline if surgery is considered in future.

mainEntity.name: Is the pelvic examination painful?

acceptedAnswer.text: The examination is usually uncomfortable rather than painful. Each step is explained throughout and a gentle, unhurried approach is used. A chaperone is always available. If you have significant vaginal atrophy, anxiety about internal examination, or a history of pelvic pain, this should be mentioned beforehand and the assessment will be adapted accordingly. There is no obligation to proceed if you are not comfortable.

mainEntity.name: Can prolapse affect the bladder?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Prolapse, particularly of the anterior vaginal wall, is frequently associated with bladder symptoms including urinary leakage on coughing or exercise, urgency and frequency, incomplete bladder emptying, and recurrent urinary tract infections. These are assessed as part of the diagnosis because some are improved by prolapse treatment, while others require separate management. Understanding the relationship between the prolapse and bladder symptoms is an important part of the assessment.

mainEntity.name: Can prolapse affect the bowel?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. A posterior vaginal wall prolapse or rectocele can be associated with constipation, difficulty emptying the bowel completely, straining, and the need to press on the vagina or perineum to defaecate. However, not all bowel symptoms with a rectocele are caused by the prolapse itself — pelvic floor dysfunction and obstructed defaecation are often separate issues. Operating on a rectocele alone does not always resolve bowel symptoms, and the underlying cause must be addressed before surgery is considered.

mainEntity.name: Will I need urodynamics?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not routinely. Urodynamics are bladder function tests indicated in selected cases — particularly where bladder symptoms are complex, mixed, or atypical; where anterior or apical prolapse repair is planned and there is a risk of unmasking or worsening stress incontinence; where there is a history of voiding difficulty or previous pelvic surgery; or where stress incontinence surgery is being considered. Urodynamics are not requested as a default — if recommended, the clinical question they are expected to answer is clearly explained.

mainEntity.name: Can I have prolapse even if it is not always visible?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Prolapse is often worse later in the day, after prolonged standing, walking, lifting, or exercise, and may be less apparent or not visible at all during a morning examination while lying down. If symptoms are typical of prolapse but the examination is inconclusive, assessment in a standing position, a repeat appointment at a different time, or greater reliance on the clinical history may be used. A negative examination does not automatically exclude prolapse.

mainEntity.name: Does a prolapse diagnosis mean I need surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A diagnosis tells you what is happening — it does not determine what to do about it. Many women manage prolapse well long-term with pelvic floor physiotherapy, vaginal oestrogen, lifestyle changes, or a vaginal pessary. Surgery is one option among several, and is recommended only when the type and severity of prolapse, functional symptoms, overall health, and the patient's own goals all support it as the right choice.

mainEntity.name: Who should assess recurrent prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Recurrent prolapse is best assessed by a subspecialist urogynaecologist, because previous surgery, tissue quality, mesh history, bladder and bowel symptoms, and future treatment options all require careful and experienced individual review. Professor Swati Jha holds RCOG subspecialty accreditation in urogynaecology and sees a significant number of recurrent prolapse cases, including women referred from other centres. She also leads the Mesh Complication Service at Sheffield Teaching Hospitals, which provides particular experience in cases where previous mesh procedures are part of the history.

mainEntity.name: What is vaginal prolapse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Vaginal prolapse occurs when the pelvic floor support structures weaken and one or more pelvic organs — the bladder, uterus, or bowel — descend into or through the vaginal canal. It affects up to half of all women who have given birth, though not all cases cause symptoms requiring treatment.

mainEntity.name: Who is the leading prolapse surgeon in Sheffield?

acceptedAnswer.text: Professor Swati Jha is a subspecialty-trained consultant urogynaecologist and Honorary Professor at the University of Sheffield, with over 15 years of dedicated experience in vaginal prolapse surgery. She holds FRCOG and RCOG subspecialty accreditation in urogynaecology, leads the urogynaecology training programme at Sheffield Teaching Hospitals, and consults privately at Spire Claremont and Circle Thornbury hospitals in Sheffield.

mainEntity.name: Can vaginal prolapse be treated without surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Many women improve significantly with pelvic floor physiotherapy, vaginal pessary fitting, vaginal oestrogen (in postmenopausal women), and lifestyle changes. I consider surgery only when symptoms are severe, worsening, or when conservative treatment has not provided adequate relief.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a GP referral to see a private gynaecologist in Sheffield?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. You can book a private consultation with me directly, without a GP referral. Contact my secretary at admin@swatijha.com or call 07990 251036.

mainEntity.name: What types of prolapse surgery are available privately in Sheffield?

acceptedAnswer.text: I offer the full range of prolapse procedures including laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy, sacrospinous fixation, hysteropexy (uterus-preserving surgery), anterior colporrhaphy, posterior colporrhaphy, and vaginal hysterectomy with pelvic floor repair. Surgery is performed at Spire Claremont and Circle Thornbury hospitals in Sheffield.

mainEntity.name: Do you use mesh in prolapse surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. I do not use mesh in my private prolapse surgery. All procedures I perform privately use the patient’s own native tissue. I lead the Mesh Complication Service at Sheffield Teaching Hospitals, where I manage complications arising from previous mesh procedures.

mainEntity.name: How long is recovery from prolapse surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Recovery depends on the procedure. Anterior or posterior repair typically requires four to six weeks before returning to non-strenuous activities. Laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy usually requires six to eight weeks. Lifting restrictions apply for at least twelve weeks following apical procedures.

acceptedAnswer.text: A new consultation costs £275. A follow-up appointment costs £160. Most major insurers are accepted including BUPA, AXA Health, Aviva, Vitality, Cigna, and WPA. No GP referral is required.
